chapter: Learning drums and Roy Eldridge's band
title: Ira Sullivan, who plays trumpet and alto
summary: Clarke praises Ira Sullivan, heard in Belgium that August, who plays trumpet and saxophones superbly, and Dance wants his name for Earl Hines.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Yeah. But that's a funny switch. Not
so many musicians will switch from reeds to brass.
Brass, yeah. Like that.
Yeah.
There's another one. What's his name? I just worked with him last -- in August. Ira. Ira -- Ira -- oh, I forgot his name. (Ira Sullivan - ed.)
You don't mean Erin?
No, Ira his name is, from Chicago.
Oh. I don't think I know.
I've never heard any musician play that good in my life.
Really? Kenny, keep close to that mike.
I've never heard anybody play that well. Both instruments.
How old is this guy?
Oh, Ira must be about -- I guess he must be 48 or 50.
Well, do think of his last name.
My God, you've got to go to hear that man.
Where did you hear him?
I heard him in Mittelheim this year. In -- we worked in the same show, in August. This past August.
Well, where is Mittelheim?
In Belgium. It's near Antwerp. Well,
the Belgian radio.
Well, where did they know of him from?
They sent all over the United States, you know, and they have scouts, you know, who search out musicians.
Well, who does this guy work with at home?
Who, Ira?
Yeah.
He's from Chicago. I don't know who he works for.
I know who would be thrilled with him. You know who's looking for a guy?
Who's that?
Earl Hines.
He is?
You must get me his name.
He's a trumpet player you never heard before. And an alto player you have never heard anything like that in your life.
But you were talking about bass.
No. I mean I was saying that musicians doubled a lot.
Yeah, I know. But does he double --
Yeah, he plays trumpet and alto.
Well, listen.
Like you never heard before.
Oh, Kenny, because you know Hines pays pretty good money now, because he's working very steady.
Yeah.
And you must give me that guy's name.
I have it at home.
Oh, you said he's a white guy.
Yeah. I have it at home on the bill, you know.
All right. Bring it tomorrow.
Yeah, I'll bring it tomorrow.
Oh, that'll be good.
And he had his group there. You never heard anything like it.
Oh, he had his group. Maybe he wouldn't want to work for --

I was amazed. I couldn't believe it. I said, 'OH, no, this is not true.' I said, 'Ira, where have you been?' He was like kind of under the weather with this drug problem, and he decided -- and he came out again.
Oh, he did?
Stronger than he ever was. That's the amazing thing about it.
Well, that's very interesting.
Oh, man. I don't know, I never heard
any kind of thing like that. Never. How extraordinary.
And he just leaves one and picks up the other.
Trumpet and alto.
And right -- soprano, right away, no fooling around, now, he just sets his lip for his embouchure, and bop, he plays.
Okay, Kenny. All right. But we were talking about guys knowing how to double in those days.
